Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01HvFcCTpW8K25m6yk3x5NYL","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. Memory\n63\tWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\n64\tan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n65\t- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n66\t\n67\t### 7. Orchestration\n68\tHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n69\t- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n70\t  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n71\t\n72\t### 8. Routing\n73\tSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n74\t- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n75\t  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n76\t\n77\t### 9. Feedback\n78\tCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\n79\tretrieval tuning, or training data.\n80\t- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n81\t  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n82\t  poisoning path.)\n83\t\n84\t## Notes\n85\t- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n86\t  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n87\t  and eval scores — from day zero.\n88\t- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n89\t  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n90\t  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n91\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"2e665576-eae4-418c-bc9b-ad9060fb1ac8","uuid":"e012bb9b-1dcf-4404-83db-01d99cbf6467","timestamp":"2026-10-03T00:24:41.858Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-pilot-core\\plugins\\p140aff59\\skills\\dependency-first-architect\\reference\\ai-systems.md","content":"# AI / agentic layer — detail\n\nLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_fszw6lywqxyl6pwmriyld3ex5lwkdxgdwyxpxec2o2pn376pv4cq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Real-time card-transaction fraud detection\n\n**Assumptions this plan depends on.** I'm stating these up front because each one changes the phase order, not just a threshold:\n- **A1. Issuer-side system.** You are an issuer or issuer-processor, and you already run an authorization switch.\n- **A2. In-path scoring is the goal.** Scoring eventually sits inside the authorization path and can approve, step up (send an extra identity check such as a one-time code or 3DS) or decline. It starts out shadow-only.\n- **A3. A fallback already exists.** Basic rules and the card networks' own scores (Visa Advanced Authorization, Mastercard Decision Intelligence) already exist, and they stay as the fallback.\n\nIf any of these is false, the plan changes:\n- **Not in-path (post-authorization alerting only):** V2 and V3 shrink to exit checks, and Phase 5 becomes \"alert routing\".\n- **Acquirer or merchant side:** the entity keys and label sources change, so V1 and the labels part of E1 change.\n- **No switch exists yet:** this becomes a different, greenfield plan.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A streaming pipeline that scores each card authorization within the switch's time budget. It combines rules and a machine-learning model, applies a decision policy (approve / step-up / decline / review), and logs every decision for disputes and retraining.\n- **Type:** Software, infrastructure and predictive ML (no LLM). Brownfield: it plugs into the existing authorization switch, disputes and chargeback systems. Not a small build: it handles real money and cardholder data under PCI DSS, and it has R3 decisions.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Latency and correctness in the authorization path, under PCI DSS compliance.\n- **Worst failure:** The in-path scorer causes mass false declines or authorization timeouts across the whole portfolio. Every cardholder's card fails at once. The control that guards this is gate V3.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Scoring latency (in-path) | Scorer p99 ≤ 50 ms, p99.9 ≤ 100 ms. Switch hard timeout 80 ms, then fail open | ASSUMPTION. Basis: common issuer practice keeps scoring to a small slice of the network's auth response window. The auth-platform owner confirms the actual remaining budget in Phase 0 | V2 |\n| Throughput | Design target 3× measured peak TPS | Peak TPS is UNKNOWN until measured from switch logs (payments ops, Phase 0), then it becomes BASELINE. The 3× is an ASSUMPTION covering seasonal peaks | V2 |\n| Availability | No reduction to the existing auth SLO. Scorer SLO 99.95% | Auth SLO is BASELINE (measured Phase 0). Scorer SLO is an ASSUMPTION: failing open covers its outages | V3 |\n| Feature freshness | Per-card velocity counters include the current transaction. Aggregate features lag ≤ 5 s | ASSUMPTION. Basis: card-testing bursts arrive seconds apart | V2 |\n| RPO / RTO | Decision log RPO 0 (dispute and audit evidence). Online feature store RTO ≤ 15 min, rebuilt by Kafka replay, with degraded scoring meanwhile | ASSUMPTION | Phase 2 drill |\n| Fraud performance | Fraud-loss basis points and acceptable false-decline rate | UNKNOWN. The fraud risk owner supplies them in Phase 1. Needed by V5 (Phase 4) and V7 (Phase 5). The current rates become BASELINE in Phase 1 | V5, V7 |\n| Storage / retention | Retention of transaction events and labels. Training needs at least 13 months to cover seasonality (ASSUMPTION) | Policy is UNKNOWN. Compliance/legal supplies it in Phase 1 | Phase 1 |\n| Resource / inference cost | Compute cost per transaction must be far below the fraud loss it prevents | UNKNOWN until V2 measures it, then checked economically in V5 | V2, V5 |\n| Operational complexity | ≤ 3 new runtime services (scorer, Flink job, online store) plus managed Kafka. On-call shared with payments ops | ASSUMPTION | Phase 2 |\n\n**Missing inputs, in order of impact:**\n1. A1–A3 above.\n2. Fraud-performance targets (fraud risk owner).\n3. The actual latency budget left in the switch (auth-platform owner).\n4. Data residency and retention (legal/compliance).\n5. Whether GDPR or a similar regime applies. That decides whether an automated decline needs legal review (V6).\n6. Which step-up channel exists today (SMS one-time code, app push or 3DS).\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Switch adapter and in-path call (Phase 0) | Change approval from the auth-switch owner and change board (CAB) | Organizational (ASSUMED needed) | Deployed |\n| Any real authorization data entering the platform | Tokenization at the switch adapter (no PAN, the full card number, leaves the switch) plus a segmented environment | Risk/security | Exposed (from Phase 0) |\n| Features, rules, labels, training (Phases 1–4) | Canonical event schema and tokenization (V1) | Decision (R3) | Specified |\n| Historical backfill and chargeback labels | Data-access approval for the warehouse and the disputes system | Organizational (ASSUMED) | Built (Phase 1) |\n| Scoring all traffic synchronously | Latency at scale (V2) | Validation | Exposed beyond allow-list |\n| Model training spec | Offline and online features match (V4) | Validation | Specified |\n| Training on cardholder data; automated declines | Legal/DPO sign-off (V6) | Organizational and risk | Committed (Phase 4) / exposed (Phase 5) |\n| Model replaces or augments rules | Model beats existing rules plus network score (V5) | Economic | Committed |\n| Any enforced decline or step-up | Fail-open behavior and decline-rate kill switch (V3) | Risk/security | Exposed |\n| Widening enforcement past the canary | Canary outcomes (V7) | Validation | Exposed |\n| Review queue in Phase 5 | Fraud-ops analyst staffing | Organizational | Exposed |\n| V5 and V7 thresholds | Targets from the fraud risk owner | Organizational | V5/V7 cannot pass without them |\n| Model training (Phase 4) | Labels at least 90 days mature | Validation (lead time, E1) | Specified |\n\nSystems that depend on the auth flow, found in Phase 0:\n- Network stand-in processing: CONFIRMED (the networks define it)\n- Disputes and chargeback system: ASSUMED\n- Existing rules engine: ASSUMED\n- Warehouse batch extracts: ASSUMED\n- Cardholder notification service: ASSUMED\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Sync vs async | R2 (changing it is a coordinated change with the switch team) | Synchronous gRPC score call from the switch with an 80 ms hard timeout. Features update asynchronously via Kafka and Flink. Decisions are logged asynchronously | The in-path budget fits | V2 | V2 fails: switch to pre-computed features only, with a lookup-only scorer. If it still fails, post-auth alerting only |\n| Failure mode on scorer error or timeout | R3 (minutes of wrong behavior cause harm at portfolio scale) | Fail open: fall back to existing rules plus network score. A decline-rate kill switch also reverts to that fallback | Fallback losses are bounded by how long the outage lasts | V3 | V3 fails, or measured fraud during fail-open windows exceeds the risk owner's limit: add a minimal high-risk fallback rule set inside the switch |\n| Consistency vs availability (online features) | R2 (feature semantics are baked into training data) | Availability: per-card counters do an atomic increment-and-read in the store. If the store is down, score with a flag saying features are missing | Bursts are caught by per-card counters, not by global consistency | V2 (burst replay) | Card-testing replay escapes because counters are stale: add read-your-writes per card |\n| Canonical event schema and entity identifiers | R3 (every feature, label and model depends on it) | ISO 8583 mapped to a versioned Avro event in a schema registry. Card is keyed by a vault token. BIN and last 4 digits kept as separate fields. Merchant, terminal and device IDs as provided | The switch supplies the fields fraud features need | V1 | V1 fails on field coverage: extend the adapter mapping before any feature is specified |\n| Data-privacy boundary (PCI DSS cardholder data) | R3 (a leaked PAN can't be taken back; storing PAN pulls the platform into scope) | PAN never leaves the switch. The fraud platform is a connected, minimized-scope system. Telemetry carries tokens only | Tokens are enough for every feature | V1 (DLP scan plus security/QSA review) | A feature needs the PAN: compute it inside the switch, never bring the PAN into the platform |\n| Training on cardholder personal data | R3 (legal commitment) | Train on tokenized, pseudonymized transaction features under the fraud-prevention legal basis. No cardholder demographics | Legal confirms the basis and the automated-decline rules | V6 | V6 fails: human review before decline, or rules-only enforcement |\n| Build vs buy (fraud platform) | R2 (in-house build is months of work but not customer-visible; a vendor contract would be R3) | Build the pipeline. Buy managed Kafka. Use network scores as model features | The team can run ML in production; the in-house build adds uplift | V5 | V5 fails twice, or the on-call budget is breached: run a vendor bake-off (Featurespace, Feedzai) on the same shadow stream |\n| Coexistence, cutover, system of record (brownfield) | R2 | The switch stays the system of record for auth outcomes. The new decision log is the record for fraud decisions. Rollout order: shadow → advisory → enforce on BIN-range canaries. Existing rules stay as the fallback | — | V3, V7 | V7 fails: revert that slice to advisory |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- Monolith vs services: one scorer service (rules, model and policy in-process), one Flink job, one batch label job.\n- Model family: gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM), compiled with Treelite.\n- Score and policy are separate: thresholds are config.\n- Infrastructure: Terraform plus ArgoCD.\n- Online store: Redis Enterprise or Aerospike.\n- Offline store and decision log: Iceberg on S3.\n\n**N/A:**\n- Prompt+RAG vs fine-tune, and hosted vs self-hosted LLM: no LLM in this system.\n- Tenancy: single issuer.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Before anything is built:**\n  - CAB approval for the switch change.\n  - A PCI-segmented Kubernetes namespace.\n  - A tokenizing adapter inside the switch, using the existing vault/HSM.\n- **The request:** A real authorization from an allow-listed internal test or employee card at a real merchant. The switch adapter tokenizes it and calls `Score` over gRPC with mTLS. The scorer applies one trivial rule, increments a per-card counter in the online store, and returns `{score, decision=APPROVE, reason_codes, model_version}`. The switch **logs the response and ignores it**: the existing path still decides.\n- **Tiers crossed:**\n  1. Switch adapter\n  2. Scorer\n  3. Online feature store\n  4. Kafka (transaction plus decision event)\n  5. Flink (updates one aggregate)\n  6. Decision log in Iceberg\n  7. A Grafana dashboard\n- **Day-zero operations:**\n  - **Deploy:** CI builds a signed image, ArgoCD deploys it, and a switch feature flag turns the call on per card token.\n  - **Logs and traces:** OpenTelemetry, with one trace ID from the switch call through the decision-log row. All logs hold tokens only.\n  - **Monitoring:** Prometheus alerts on scorer p99, timeout rate and Flink lag.\n  - **Rollback:** flip the switch flag off, plus an ArgoCD rollback to the previous image.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed card tokens behind the switch flag. Responses are not acted on.\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- One real authorization produces one trace across all 7 tiers.\n- A deploy and a rollback both go through the pipeline.\n- Injecting 200 ms of scorer latency makes the switch time out, fail open and fire the alert.\n- Baselines recorded: scorer p50/p99 at near-zero load, auth p99 and peak TPS from switch logs, and the auth SLO.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Data contract, full shadow mirror, labels**\n  - Unlocks: specifying features, rules and the model; measured baselines for fraud and false declines.\n  - Depends on: Phase 0 and V0; data-access approval.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Freeze the V1 schema in the registry, with compatibility mode BACKWARD.\n    2. Run the V1 replay and DLP scan.\n    3. Mirror **all** auth traffic asynchronously to Kafka, out of the auth path.\n    4. Start label ingestion (E1): fraud-coded chargebacks, cardholder fraud claims, Visa TC40 / Mastercard SAFE reports. Join them to the decision log by transaction ID.\n    5. Backfill 13 or more months of history (tokenized) from the warehouse.\n    6. Get fraud-performance targets from the risk owner, and retention and residency from legal.\n    7. Start V6.\n  - Rollback: turn the mirror off. Nothing is in the path. The schema evolves only through registry versions.\n  - Exit check: V1 passes; baseline fraud basis points and false-decline rate are published; risk-owner targets are recorded with their labels.\n\n- **Phase 2: Defenses and budgets in the path**\n  - Unlocks: synchronous shadow scoring on all traffic.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1 and V1.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Circuit breaker and timeout in the switch adapter; fail open to the existing decision.\n    2. Decline-rate and step-up-rate kill switch: compare the 1-minute rate to baseline and auto-revert to the fallback.\n    3. Input validation. Out-of-range or malformed fields get a \"degraded\" flag and are never used for a hard decline.\n    4. Four-eyes approval and audit for every rule or threshold change.\n    5. V2 load test with burst replay.\n    6. Widen synchronous shadow scoring from the allow-list to 1%, then 10%, then 100%, with decisions still ignored.\n    7. Online-store recovery drill (RTO).\n  - Rollback: switch flag per traffic slice.\n  - Exit check: V2 passes. V3 runs on shadow traffic, and its kill-switch trip is rehearsed. Auth p99 is within baseline + 5 ms at 100% shadow (an ASSUMPTION; confirm with the switch owner).\n\n- **Phase 3: Features and rules (shadow)**\n  - Unlocks: rules-based decisions ready for advisory; training data for the model.\n  - Depends on: Phase 2 and V2.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. One shared feature-definition library used by Flink and the offline backfill: velocity (per card, merchant, device, BIN), geo-distance, merchant category risk, card-present vs card-not-present, network scores.\n    2. Run V4.\n    3. Port existing rules into the scorer's rules engine, run them in shadow, and compare against the existing engine's decisions.\n    4. Stream advisory reason codes to the analyst case queue.\n  - Rollback: features are versioned. A feature-set flag pins the previous version.\n  - Exit check: V4 passes. Shadow rules agree with existing-engine decisions ≥ 99.5% (ASSUMPTION), with differences explained.\n\n- **Phase 4: Model**\n  - Unlocks: model-driven scores.\n  - Depends on: Phase 3 and V4; V6; labels at least 90 days mature (E1).\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Train LightGBM on out-of-time splits. Register it in MLflow with data snapshot, feature version and code hash.\n    2. Derive reason codes (SHAP top-k).\n    3. Run V5.\n    4. Serve it in-process in shadow and confirm V2 latency still holds with the model loaded.\n  - Rollback: the model registry pins the previous version, and the model can be swapped by config.\n  - Exit check: V5 and V6 pass, and the V2 re-run with the model loaded passes.\n\n- **Phase 5: Enforcement rollout (exposure smallest first)**\n  - Unlocks: real fraud prevention.\n  - Depends on: Phase 4, V3, V5, V6; analysts staffed.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Advisory: decisions go to analysts only.\n    2. Enforce **step-up** on a 1% BIN-range canary for 14 days and run V7.\n    3. Then enforce **decline** at the top score band on the same canary.\n    4. Widen 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, re-running V7 at each step.\n    5. Cardholder notification and an analyst override path.\n  - Rollback: flip a slice back to advisory through the policy config, in seconds. No point of no return: the existing rules are never removed (see §10).\n  - Exit check: V7 passes at each widening; 100% of traffic is enforced.\n\n- **Phase 6: Champion/challenger and retraining loop**\n  - Unlocks: sustained performance under drift.\n  - Depends on: Phase 5 and V7.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Challenger model in shadow on 100% of traffic.\n    2. Drift monitors (population stability index on features and scores).\n    3. Scheduled retraining on matured labels. Analyst labels go through review, never straight into training.\n    4. Promote a challenger only through a V5 re-run plus a canary.\n  - Rollback: the previous champion is pinned.\n  - Exit check: one full retrain → V5 → canary → promotion cycle completes, traced and audited.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | §4 | §4 exit check | Trace export, ArgoCD history, alert record in the change ticket | Phase 1. If it fails: fix before anything else | 0 |\n| V1 | The canonical schema carries every fraud-relevant field and no PAN | Replay 7 days of production auth messages through the mapper; run a DLP scan over Kafka, the online store, Iceberg and logs; security architect plus QSA review | ≥ 99.99% of messages parse (ASSUMPTION). Required-field null rates within spec. **Zero cleartext PAN** (REQUIREMENT: PCI DSS v4.0 Req. 3: PAN unreadable wherever stored). Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | PAN stays in the switch; mTLS; segmented namespace; secrets in Vault; card allow-list | One OpenTelemetry trace across all tiers; latency and timeout alerts; logs hold tokens only | Terraform and ArgoCD; signed images; the version of every deployed component is recorded | Timeout plus fail open; rollback by flag |\n| 1 | DLP scan (V1); least-privilege access to backfill data; retention tags | Kafka/Flink lag; label-join coverage dashboard; baseline fraud metrics | Schema registry versions; backfill snapshot IDs | Mirror is off-path; Kafka replication factor 3 |\n| 2 | Four-eyes rule/threshold changes with audit; input validation | Decline-rate and step-up-rate monitors feed the kill switch; per-slice latency | Load-test scenarios in version control | Circuit breaker; kill switch; store recovery drill (RTO) |\n| 3 | Rule authors' access controlled by role; feature access limited to tokens | Per-feature null/drift panels; shadow agreement dashboard | Shared feature library; versioned feature sets | Degraded-feature flag never drives a hard decline |\n| 4 | Training environment segmented; model artifacts signed | Score distribution; reason-code frequencies | MLflow: data snapshot, code hash, hyperparameters, feature version | Previous model pinned; swap by config |\n| 5 | Override path audited; cardholder notification without PAN | Canary vs control dashboards; complaint feed | Policy config versioned per slice | Per-slice revert to advisory in seconds |\n| 6 | Analyst labels reviewed before training (blocks poisoning) | Drift (PSI) alerts; champion vs challenger panels | Retraining pipeline is deterministic from snapshot IDs | Promotion only through V5 plus canary; champion pinned |\n\n## 8.
